newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh execution may be faster than usual.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh execution may be faster than usual.

text.p: In a country where prisoners on death row sometimes languish for a decade or more, Timothy McVeigh -- the worst mass murderer in American history -- may be put to death comparatively quickly.

"This is not going to be a long appeals process compared to some that go on for 10 to 12 years," University of Colorado law professor William Pizzi said of the man sentenced to death on Friday for blowing up the Oklahoma city federal building, killing 168 people -- more Americans than in the Gulf War.

Legal experts said McVeigh's death by lethal injection could come within a few years, depending on the length of the appeals process that automatically kicks in after a jury of seven men and five women sentenced him to death for the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P.Murrah federal building.

McVeigh, 29, now joins 13 other prisoners who have been sentenced to die for federal crimes, mostly for drug-related offences. Throughout the country there are about 3,200 prisoners on death row who have been sentenced to die for state crimes.

The jurors in the Oklahoma bombing trial made their decision after hearing from 38 prosecution witnesses who either survived the bombing, lost a loved one, or were sent to the bombing site as a rescue worker.

McVeigh's lawyers pleaded for a life sentence, putting Army friends of the Gulf War veteran on the stand to describe him as a model soldier and war hero. Boyhood friends talked about a happy, sweet-natured child growing up in a rural area near Buffalo, New York.
McVeigh's conviction and his death sentence will be automatically appealed to the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals in Denver.

While the appeals go on, the state of Oklahoma has vowed to put McVeigh on trial for murder and McVeigh's alleged co-conspirator, Terry Nichols, will be tried in a separate federal court trial. He has pleaded not guilty.
Legal experts said the defence has little chance of overturning McVeigh's guilty verdict.

The trial judge Richard Matsch is highly respected and lawyers praised his handling of the case and preventing it from becoming a circus. He slapped a sweeping gag order on the attorneys in the case, kept the identity of jurors secret and the pace of the trial moving along.

"I would say his reputation is that he is very highly thought of by the Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit. That leads me to think they (appeals court) would be very inclined to uphold the verdicts," Pizzi said.

McVeigh's lawyers could then ask the U.S. Supreme Court to review the case. But Scott Robinson, a Denver trial attorney who analysed the bombing trial, said less than one percent of such petitions were granted. "Chances are good they won't take it. If they take the case then that delays things another year and a half," Robinson said.

But he added that one area of possible appeal was the judge's decision not to force government intelligence agencies to turn over volumes of classified information. The defence had claimed that international terrorists could have been behind the bombing.
Robert Precht, Director of the Office of Public Service at the University of Michigan, agreed, saying, "I would expect there will be some very substantial issues raised on appeal."

Several issues that could be appealed would be the judge's decision to exclude certain evidence about errors at the Federal Bureau of Investigation crime laboratory and whether McVeigh could receive a fair trial given the intense publicity surrounding the case, Precht said.
Besides the legal avenues, the high-profile case is sure to put the spotlight on the death penalty once again.
Earlier this week, Archbishop Charles Chaput of the Catholic Diocese of Denver, voiced concern at what he called a "vengeful" spirit in society.
Since the United States resumed executions in 1976, there have been 391 executions, most by lethal injection.
Public approval of capital punishment in most recent polls runs at around 75 percent.
